title: Applied anatomy: the popliteal fossa and common peroneal nerve

related.why: Same method for the upper limb: map the deficit onto the nerve

brief.scenario: A 35-year-old footballer had his right knee forced backwards and inwards in a tackle. His knee is swollen and he now has a foot drop. This is a verbal viva: the examiner will ask about the popliteal fossa and will read out a description of a dissection.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the popliteal fossa and the common peroneal nerve, including the written description the examiner reads out, and relate them to his injury.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Diamond, contents, then the nerve round the fibular neck. Keep the artery in mind.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating it as a nerve problem only. A knee that bent this way may have dislocated and reduced.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "The popliteal fossa is a diamond: hamstrings above, gastrocnemius below."

grid.label: Borders
grid.fail: Names 'the hamstrings' as one border, or cannot name the lower borders.
grid.pass: Upper lateral: biceps femoris. Upper medial: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Lower: medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius.
grid.high: Adds plantaris laterally below; roof of fascia pierced by the small saphenous vein; floor of femur, posterior capsule and popliteus.

grid.label: Contents
grid.pass: Superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery. Common peroneal nerve along the medial edge of biceps femoris.
grid.high: Explains the artery is tethered at the adductor hiatus and the soleal arch, so it tears when the knee dislocates.

grid.label: Course of the nerve
grid.fail: Cannot say where the nerve is most at risk.
grid.pass: Leaves the sciatic nerve, follows biceps femoris, winds round the fibular neck, then divides into deep and superficial branches.
grid.high: At the fibular neck it is superficial, on bone and tethered: at risk from fractures, plaster, tight bandages and varus knee injury.

grid.label: Motor loss
grid.pass: Deep branch: tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus. Superficial branch: peroneus longus and brevis (eversion).
grid.high: Adds extensor digitorum brevis, and that inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) is spared.

grid.label: Sensory loss
grid.fail: Says the sole is numb, or maps the whole foot.
grid.pass: Deep branch: first web space. Superficial branch: lower lateral leg and most of the dorsum of the foot.
grid.high: Adds the lateral sural cutaneous nerve (upper lateral calf) from the main trunk; sole (tibial) and lateral foot (sural) spared.

grid.label: Nerve or root
grid.fail: Cannot separate a peroneal palsy from an L5 root lesion.
grid.pass: An L5 root lesion also weakens inversion and hip abduction; a peroneal palsy spares both.
grid.high: Adds back pain and positive straight leg raise in radiculopathy; nerve conduction studies to confirm the level.

grid.label: Vascular safety
grid.fail: Accepts palpable foot pulses as excluding arterial injury.
grid.pass: Treats it as a possible spontaneously reduced knee dislocation: pulses, capillary refill and ankle-brachial pressure index; vascular opinion if abnormal.
grid.high: States an index below 0.9 needs CT angiography, and that normal pulses do not exclude an intimal tear.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What are the borders of the popliteal fossa?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The hamstrings above and the calf below.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What lies in it, from superficial to deep?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The popliteal artery is most superficial, then the vein and nerve.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Where is the common peroneal nerve most at risk?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Behind the knee, in the middle of the fossa.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd ask him to lift his foot up.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: On the sole of the foot.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: His foot pulses are palpable. Anything else about the circulation?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, if the pulses are there the artery is fine.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the borders of the popliteal fossa?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It's a diamond. Above and laterally, biceps femoris. Above and medially, semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Below, the medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: From superficial to deep: the tibial nerve, the popliteal vein, then the popliteal artery. The common peroneal nerve runs along the medial edge of biceps femoris.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It leaves the sciatic nerve, follows biceps femoris, winds round the neck of the fibula and divides into deep and superficial branches.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you test the motor supply?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Deep branch: dorsiflexion with tibialis anterior, and toe extension. Superficial branch: eversion with peroneus longus and brevis.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: First web space for the deep branch. Lower lateral leg and most of the dorsum of the foot for the superficial branch.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you tell this from an L5 root lesion?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: An L5 lesion also weakens inversion and hip abduction. A peroneal palsy spares both.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: His foot pulses are palpable. Is the circulation safe?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not necessarily. His knee may have dislocated and gone back. I'd check capillary refill and the ankle-brachial pressure index, and get a vascular opinion if it's abnormal.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Biceps femoris above and laterally, semimembranosus and semitendinosus above and medially, the two heads of gastrocnemius below, with plantaris laterally. The roof is fascia, pierced by the small saphenous vein. The floor is the femur, the posterior capsule and popliteus.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why does it matter where the artery lies?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's deepest, and it's tethered at the adductor hiatus above and the soleal arch below. So when the knee dislocates it stretches and tears.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why is the nerve injured at the fibula?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It lies superficially on bone and is tethered as it winds round the neck, so fractures, plaster, tight bandages and a varus injury like his can all damage it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd also feel extensor digitorum brevis on the dorsum of the foot, and check inversion. Inversion is tibialis posterior on the tibial nerve, so it should be normal.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The lateral sural cutaneous nerve comes off the main trunk and supplies the upper lateral calf. The sole and the lateral border of the foot should be spared.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: And if you suspected a root lesion?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd ask about back pain, do a straight leg raise, and confirm the level with nerve conduction studies.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: An index below 0.9 needs CT angiography. Pulses can be present with an intimal tear, so I'd get a vascular opinion now.

failures.move: Accepting foot pulses as proof the artery is intact.
failures.consequence: Misses an intimal tear after a reduced dislocation, which can thrombose and threaten the limb.
Cannot tell deep from superficial branch involvement, or nerve from root.
Cannot separate a peroneal palsy from an L5 radiculopathy.
Misunderstands why the artery is injured in dislocation.

recovery.when: You forget the order of contents
recovery.line: Nerve, vein, artery, from superficial to deep: the artery is deepest, on the floor.

recovery.when: Asked about a knee injury with foot drop
recovery.line: I'd treat this as a possible knee dislocation until the artery is cleared.

knowledge.fact: Borders: biceps femoris; semimembranosus and semitendinosus; two heads of gastrocnemius.
Contents superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery.
Deep peroneal: dorsiflexors and first web space. Superficial peroneal: evertors, lower lateral leg, dorsum of foot.
Inversion (tibialis posterior) is spared in peroneal palsy but weak in an L5 root lesion.
After knee dislocation, an ankle-brachial index below 0.9 needs arterial imaging.

recall.think: Foot drop after a knee injury: nerve, and is the artery intact?
recall.say: "Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck."
do: Map first web space and dorsum
recall.trap: Palpable pulses do not exclude arterial injury.
recall.finish: Vascular opinion if ABPI abnormal; nerve conduction studies for the nerve.

partner.opening: This is a verbal viva on the back of a right knee. Tell me the borders of the popliteal fossa.

reveals.finding: Read out: in a posterior dissection of the right popliteal fossa, the deepest structure lies directly on the floor of the fossa, against the back of the femur and the knee capsule. It is a thick-walled vessel, continuous above with the vessel passing through an opening in adductor magnus. Ask: what is it, and what lies superficial to it?
Dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion MRC 2. Inversion and plantarflexion normal.
Reduced sensation over the lower lateral leg, dorsum of the foot and first web space. Sole normal.

push.question: What are the borders?
push.expect: Biceps femoris; semimembranosus and semitendinosus; two heads of gastrocnemius.

push.question: Name the contents from superficial to deep.
push.expect: Tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery; common peroneal on biceps femoris.

push.question: Why is the nerve injured at the fibular neck?
How would you tell this from an L5 root lesion?
push.expect: Inversion and hip abduction weak in L5; spared in peroneal palsy.

push.question: Is his circulation safe?
push.expect: Possible reduced dislocation; ABPI; below 0.9 needs CT angiography.

curveballs.prompt: Only the first web space is numb and eversion is normal.
curveballs.safeAnswer: An isolated deep peroneal nerve lesion; the superficial branch is spared.

curveballs.prompt: Foot pulses are present but the ABPI is 0.8.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Arterial injury is not excluded. CT angiography and an urgent vascular opinion.

curveballs.prompt: Why is the foot held plantarflexed and inverted?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Dorsiflexors and evertors are lost; plantarflexors and tibialis posterior (tibial nerve) act unopposed.
